label.trigger: The local side begins the closing handshake (WriteMessage or WriteControl with a CloseMessage), keeps the default close handler, and then reads the connection until the peer's answering close frame arrives, which is the normal shutdown sequence of a client.
label.expected_impact: Sending the first close frame makes every later write fail with ErrCloseSent. When the reply arrives, the default handler tries to echo a close frame, gets that sentinel and passes it up, so NextReader/ReadMessage return ErrCloseSent instead of the promised *CloseError. IsCloseError and IsUnexpectedCloseError then misclassify an orderly shutdown and applications log or count it as a failure.

context_locations.note: The package documentation is the contract: a received close frame must surface from the read methods as a *CloseError, whatever the handler had to do.
After a close frame goes out through WriteMessage (WriteControl does the same further down), the connection stores ErrCloseSent as its sticky write error.
WriteControl hands back that stored error before writing anything, so the handler's attempt to answer is guaranteed to fail on the side that started the handshake.

known_counterevidence.note: The default ping handler already treats the sentinel as harmless; a report about pong replies is not this defect, it only shows the pattern the close handler lacks.
A connection whose peer starts the handshake is unaffected: nothing was sent yet, the echo succeeds and the reader gets the *CloseError.

label.fix_summary: In the default close handler keep the WriteControl result and ignore it when it equals ErrCloseSent (our close frame is already out, so there is nothing left to answer); still return any other write error.

check.summary: An adaptation of the test added by the fix (new name, named close-code constant): over in-memory buffers the client sends a normal close, the server reads it and its default handler answers, then the client reads; both reads must yield a CloseError with code 1000.
